title: The gerund: two actions at the same time

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know the gerund for actions at the same time (*Llegó corriendo*, *Volvimos a casa cantando*) from B1 Unit 2, and *estar* + gerund from A1 Unit 19. In history it shows how or why someone acted: the gerund and the main verb have the same subject.

sections.title: Gerund + main verb
rows: Esperando liberarse…, los tlaxcaltecas se unieron a Cortés.
Hoping to free themselves…: the reason, in the gerund.
Trabajando como intérprete, Malintzin ayudó a Cortés.
Working as an interpreter…: the way she helped.
…los chichimecas atacaron los caminos, moviéndose en grupos pequeños.
The gerund can also come after the main verb.

items.spanish: Esperando liberarse de los mexicas, los tlaxcaltecas se unieron a Cortés.
items.english: Hoping to free themselves from the Mexica, the Tlaxcalans joined Cortés.

items.spanish: Trabajando como intérprete, Malintzin ayudó a Cortés.
items.english: Working as an interpreter, Malintzin helped Cortés.

items.spanish: Los españoles avanzaban hacia el norte, buscando plata.
items.english: The Spaniards advanced north, looking for silver.

items.spanish: Los chichimecas atacaban los caminos, moviéndose en grupos pequeños.
items.english: The Chichimecas attacked the roads, moving in small groups.

sections.content: Add *-ando* to *-ar* verbs and *-iendo* to *-er* and *-ir* verbs. The person who does the gerund is the subject of the main verb. A gerund never says "before": for an earlier action use *antes de* + infinitive instead.
